I do not know how I will afford rent, savings for the future, taking care of my parents -- I am the only child. I do not know whether I can land an industry job in the competitive environment over-producing PhDs.  I heard about people who get scholarships and earn 30-50% above the typical postdoc salary. They apply for grants and quickly become PIs to earn their lower three figures. Or they aim for green cards through H1B or EB2, paying for the mistake of being born in a shit third-world country, through living off $45k for several years to then end a better paying job in industry. Both options require publishing at least three first author papers, having citations, getting funding, networking -- all the things I don't see myself doing as of now. There are labs that are more collaborative and people end up helping with other peoples' projects and with more papers in the end. I am not in one of them. Q41.original_text: I would most like to work as a researcher in a national lab (like NASA) or a non-profit research institute. I have not dismissed the idea completely in continuing in academia, but I have seen how, at least on the lower level (assistant professor, etc), the goals of pursuing research do not align with mine, or what I believed of academia before pursuing an advanced degree. There is too much focus on pursuing ideas that are "known" to succeed. Funding is only handed out to those projects that are likely to succeed, leaving out the well explained/though out ideas that have a high chance of failure. I don't really think non-academic research institutes are any different. I am not well versed in the structure and expectations of non-academic research institutes, but I know that academia isn't quite the right fit. Other universities, and certainly for those academics who have already proven themselves, might adhere more to my thoughts on the pursuit of knowledge, but for the foreseeable future I want to try somewhere new.  Ideally, I'd like to be an astronaut, but as that is extremely unlikely, I'm interested in getting to pursue ideas with other motivated, intelligent collaborators that push the boundaries of knowledge for the sake of curiosity.

Q60.original_text: The feedback loop between researchers and potential funding agencies is slowly closing off potentially fruitful research avenues because of fads that are relying too heavily on people who are not qualified to determine the future of research (e.g. politicians). I am in a relatively young field so I've had the opportunity to watch the foundations get built, and see newly anointed professors start their labs. From what I've seen, the foundations are flashy and weak. They focus on what will capture the public's attention without regards to the fundamental science, and at some point the foundation will collapse because the fad will fade and the flash has nothing to fall back on when extinguished. However, no jobs (or funding) is available unless you can blind those in charge with a flashy demo that has no real substance. I fear this is a general trend that will only get worse as the population of those who abhor intelligence and curiosity grows and continue to appoint like minded individuals to positions of power. It is a vicious cycle that is heading for collapse, unless enough people can band together to preserve the pursuit of knowledge for the sake of knowledge This was what I thought academia was, until I was embedded in the midst of it, and saw how very petty academia can be.

Unfortunately, moral standards at some German institutions are at its lowest level: A new research institute that is yet to receive its academic recognition will rather ignore repeated complaints on staff injustice and academic misconduct than risk a bad reputation. Likewise, a young PI will refuse to protect and stand behind a victim of sabotage and pretend all is fine, as long as there is a possibility for a new publication from the person doing the injustice.       PhD students are often subjected to exploitation with no protection since at the end of the day everyone needs that critical reference letter to pursue the next step in an academic career.

Q55.text: There are far more opportunities available for postgraduate students in the USA/EU, many of my friends and colleagues in the field who did their Masters degree abroad easily found PhD positions at top ranking institutions despite having no publications in the field (or often any publications at all) and mediocre grades. As a department we also regularly experience what we perceive as discrimination from reviewers towards third world universities, even when the results are objectively valuable and can be quickly reproduced with no effort (such as running a script with fully free and open source code). Many reviewers force us to cite their own papers in the manuscript before accepting our publication (despite being anonymous it is obvious when the authorship fields of these papers all contain the same researcher). Often the work is not significant or the results are less competative than other papers already cited in the manuscript.  In short it is very difficult (but certainly possible) to get in to the right networks for your career if you're coming from the wrong institution. The quality of your research is largely irrelevant, even in fields where problems have objective and established metrics for the quality of solutions.

Q26.text: As a PhD student I have to collect a certain amount of points in order to be able to complete a PhD study program. Those points can be obtained from a variety of activities like attending conferences/meetings, courses (both directly related to the thesis topic or focusing on soft skills development) or having papers published. Only students who complete the study program can submit their thesis. University requirement for the thesis is to have at least one paper accepted, however there is an unwritten rule in my lab that students need to have at least 2 accepted papers one submitted and one ready to be send. The submitted thesis (approved by supervisor)  is being revised by internal committee (experts in the field from the University) and once approved is being send to the external committee members (experts in the field from outside the University). Only when the thesis is approved by the external committee members the public defense can take place. So obtaining a PhD degree at the University I am currently studding is a complex and multitask challenge.

Q26.original_text: My experience is both good and bad - but I have changed a a supervisor and a project in the middle of my PhD as with  the first one it was not possible to work. The person was manipulative, changing mind and also a bully. The great science in the lab turned out to be well sold bullshit with  low n... Luckily the people in the doctoral school helped me and supported me to change. The second supervisor was a really good human being. I could come back to a normal mental state during work with that person.  He also allowed me to do the work and truly lead my project. Still, he was not great in all of the aspects, but I learned to work with him and overall we have really good relationship. A part of it is knowing a limit of the other person and knowing how much you need to put effort to get the lead or advice. SO in my experience the system is not that bad, but there are bad people. I was highly motivated to obtain my PhD diploma - working a lot and did not drop after the first supervisor, but I went through a lot including a bit of depression, sleeping problems even occasional bedwetting at age of 28!!! It also almost caused a breaking of my personal relationship, which I still am working on... The people who helped me to get out of this toxic situation were advisors in my doctoral program. At some point after the weekly seminar when we had beer in our classroom an advisor would simply ask me how am I and how my PhD is going. Well, after a few sentences I started crying and this is how weekly meetings would started with me and the advisor to get help. To learn what is wrong, to help my mental health and to find a good solution. It was not easy but the fact that someone just heard me out and understood (did not deny or ignore it) make me stronger and capable to take steps to exit. There was no path which would be decided but they helped me to take decisions  to get through it and treat me seriously. So if I could summ up somehow - PhD programs needs advisors (separately from supervisors) who will be able to build trust and will truly care for the students. My PhD program has this position since a few years. My doctoral program hass better achievements of the PhD student then other programs in France as evaluations shows (Former FdV now FIRE doctroral program). In my opinion it is because they truly care about the students, their mental state and are supportive. During all 4 years of PhD we would have quite a lot 'soft-skills' classes where we were made aware about the fact that we have broad opportunities outside science (so helpful to know even if you want to stay in science), how maintain work-life balance, self presentation and what saved me and my PhD  - they talked with us often. I sow other stories like mine ending not that well just because there were not this support net around in other doctoral programs or often students were not aware that they can feel bad and can just talk with the advisor.   For me the academic system is sth different from graduate program but this could be because this looks like that in France. You belong to a lab where you do your PhD scientific project but Gradschool is a different thing - in another building. And the fact that we had a place to gather, meet and that we were forced to interact with each other build a community which at the end is really helpful. The fact that there are other people who will take your side and also advice you and guide or colleagues.  What is important the people were competent- so it was not a place just to complain on your supervisor or lab but they always gave constructive advice and you felt that they are there for you to keep you in a good shape, scientifically and mentally. Even if this needs quitting PhD or doing less ambitious things. But it always your decision. And your needs that are important without compromising  high scientific standards.

Q60.text: Thanks for performing this survey. This is an extremely important topic that is often overlooked. We are looked at as cheap labor (and often young) labor that needs to pay their dues. But often it comes at the cost of our mental and physical health. My mental and physical health has significantly declined over the past 4 years that I've been in my PhD program. I've definitely experienced depression and anxiety, and have had many more visits to the doctor for physical health problems. A back problem from sitting for 12 hours a day at the computer, problems with my hands from typing so much, other problems from increasing my drinking (to cope with stress), a urinary tract infection from holding my urine too long because I don't have time to pee because I am working; I've often put off medical appointments due to lack of time as well. Students often put off their health like they are in survival mode and tell themselves "it's okay to not be healthy for a while" because when you are done with the program you will have time to be healthy. But after years of putting off your health and happiness, living in "survival mode" becomes unbearable. That combined with feeling like you have no control over your own labor nor are getting compensated a livable wage for it can be extremely depressing. Granted some students are predisposed to having more health problems than others as a result of the stressors of a PhD program--however, there are major problems with the system and culture of PhD education that need to be fixed to support student health.

De plus, il semble y avoir une certaine « game politique » afin d'optimiser ses chances d'obtenir des subventions. Ainsi, dès lors qu'un professeur respecte ses valeurs fondamentales qui l'empêchent de jouer cette « game politique », il devient très difficile pour lui de faire rouler efficacement son laboratoire, ce qui est notre cas. Au cours des années, faute de financement, nous avons perdu des techniciens et des associés de recherche pour nous aider dans nos travaux, diminuant ainsi notre capacité à produire des publications de qualité. Or, le système actuel semble juger la valeur d'un groupe de recherche presque exclusivement sur le nombre de publications que ce dernier produit (et pas nécessairement sur le nombre de publications de qualité), ce qui nous fait entrer dans un cercle vicieux dont il est presque impossible de sortir. Ayant choisi mes études supérieures en fonction de mes intérêts et non du succès du groupe de recherche, mes possibilités de publication tôt dans mes études ont été inexistantes, m'empêchant par le fait même d'avoir accès à la majorité des bourses d'études qui évaluent le potentiel de recherche d'un candidat en fonction de son nombre de publications. Avoir su cela plus tôt, j'aurais dû faire une maîtrise dans un gros groupe de recherche connaissant du succès afin que mon nom apparaisse sur plusieurs publications. Une chance que mon université m'aide financièrement, car sinon je n'aurais jamais pu faire la recherche que je fais actuellement.

Q26.text: O sistema acadêmico da república tcheca é bastante focado em produção.  Não se importa muito a defesa de uma tese, da ideia em si.  Apenas vejo que o programas de PhD em geral esqueceram da onde vem a sigla Ph.D e não discutem mais as coisas no âmbito argumentativo.  Não importam tanto com o racional do projeto, com a hipótese do projeto... e a defesa argumentativa que deveria ser feita.  Maioria dos projetos vejo que começa simplesmente por que temos dinheiro e estrutura. Mas não porque temos um grande racional e uma justificativa para tentar lançar uma hipótese a ser defendida por provas a posteriori.    Na minha concepção,  Tudo deveria iniciar com uma ideia sólida.  Uma hipótese a qual todos não consigam derrubar com argumentos. Sendo interessante alocar recursos escassos para responder uma pergunta da qual necessita-se de uma resposta a posteriori.    O sistema então acaba valorizando bastante dados soltos, contudo ainda sim são resultados. E acaba desvalorizando o tempo 'perdido' no campo das ideias.   A quantidade muitas vezes parece ser mais importante do que a qualidade . Infelizmente vejo que o sistema recompensa este tipo de mentalidade.  No Brasil (país onde fiz meu mestrado), não era diferente.   Com isso , o sistema que criamos é um sistema preocupado com técnicos. Pessoas que vangloriam por saber determinada técnica.  Pois em teoria, isto traz mais produção.  As pessoas não entendem que aprender técnica é apenas uma questão de tempo e prática. Não precisa de raciocínio lógico. Sendo que em muitos institutos grandes, você de fato tem técnicos e facilities para fazer o trabalho técnico para você.   No entanto, técnica pode ser aplicada mil vezes... mas se não estiver denfendendo uma ideia não fará nenhum sentido fazer por fazer.   Acredito que precisamos fazer um esforço para mudar esta mentalidade nos institutos ao redor do mundo.  A revista Nature é muito conceituada e acredito que ela representa bem a amostragem dos institutos que de fato estão preocupados em mover o mundo através de ideias.    Pedro Zeni
